title: Repo rate hike or cut: what it does to your home loan EMI
seoTitle: Repo Rate Hike and Your Home Loan EMI: What Changes
h1: Repo rate hike or cut: what it does to your home loan EMI
metaDescription: How a repo rate hike or cut reaches your home loan EMI: EBLR and spread, what 0.25% costs in rupees, why banks stretch the tenure, and your options at reset.
excerpt: A 0.25% repo change adds about ₹775 a month to a ₹50 lakh loan, or a whole extra year if the bank stretches the tenure. How it works and what to ask for.
targetAudience: Indian home loan borrowers on floating rates wondering how an RBI decision changes their EMI
sourceVideoTitle: Will Your Home Loan EMI Finally Reduce? 🚨 RBI Repo Rate Explained
author: Muthu

faq.question: How much will my EMI increase if the repo rate goes up by 0.25%?
faq.answer: On a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan at 7.75%, by about ₹775 a month if the tenure stays the same. Later in the loan the increase is smaller. Many banks keep the EMI and add about a year to the tenure instead, which costs more in total interest.

faq.question: When will a repo rate change affect my home loan?
faq.answer: At your loan's next reset date. Repo-linked loans must be reset at least once every three months, so the change usually reaches you within that period. Older MCLR or base-rate loans follow the bank's own benchmark and can lag further.

faq.question: Why did my loan tenure increase instead of my EMI?
faq.answer: Banks often keep the EMI unchanged and extend the number of EMIs when rates rise. RBI rules let you choose a higher EMI, a longer tenure or a mix, so you can ask the bank to raise the EMI instead.

faq.question: What is the spread on a home loan?
faq.answer: It's the part of your rate above the bank's benchmark, set mainly by your credit risk. It stays fixed for your loan unless your credit assessment changes substantially. A repo change moves the benchmark, not your spread.

faq.question: Should I reduce my EMI or tenure when rates fall?
faq.answer: Keeping the EMI and shortening the tenure saves more interest. Lowering the EMI frees monthly cash. If you have no tight budget, keep the EMI.
